[[Category:Large language models]]
[[Category:Natural language processing]]
A '''large language model''' ('''LLM''') is an [[artificial intelligence]] system built as a [[neural network]] with a very large parameter count, typically based on the [[Transformer]] architecture, trained by [[machine learning]] on broad text corpora to generate text in response to prompts.<ref>{{#cite:Q3130}}</ref> This self-supervised objective, usually [[next-token prediction]], requires no human labels because the supervision signal is derived from the text itself.

== Architecture and pretraining objective ==

At the time of writing (2026-08), the most widely adopted LLMs are Transformer models, specifically autoregressive decoder-only Transformers.<ref>{{#cite:Q3130}}</ref> Given a token sequence $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_T)$, the pretraining objective maximises the conditional likelihood

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}}
=
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\log P(x_t \mid x_{1:t-1}; \theta),
$$

where $\theta$ denotes the model parameters. The term for $t=1$ is conditioned on the empty context $x_{1:0}$, supplied in practice by a begin-of-sequence token. The causal attention mask ensures that the prediction for position $t$ depends only on $x_{1:t-1}$, not on future tokens.

== Scaling laws ==

The performance of LLMs improves predictably with model size, training-data volume, and computational budget, a relationship known as '''scaling laws'''.<ref>{{#cite:Q3141}}</ref> Language-model loss follows a power law in compute $C$,

$$
L(C)=aC^{-\alpha},
\qquad \alpha\approx 0.05,
$$

so diminishing returns are intrinsic: halving the loss would require roughly $10^{6}$ times more compute. The [[Chinchilla scaling laws|Chinchilla prescription]] refines this picture by balancing parameters and data, recommending approximately 20 tokens per parameter.<ref>{{#cite:Q3164}}</ref> The finite supply of high-quality public text, however, places a practical ceiling on data scaling, with estimates suggesting a “data wall” may arrive by the late 2020s.<ref>{{#cite:Q3181}}</ref>

== Data scaling and the data wall ==

Let $N$ denote the number of trainable parameters, $D$ the number of training tokens, and $C$ the computational budget. Under a fixed $C$, the [[Chinchilla scaling laws|Chinchilla prescription]] approximates the compute-optimal allocation by

$$
D \approx 20N.
$$

Because high-quality public text is finite, data scaling cannot continue indefinitely at fixed $N$. If $D_{\max}$ is the available token stock, a data-constrained loss model is

$$
L_{\text{data}}(N,D_{\max})
=
L_{\infty}
+
\left(\frac{N_c}{N}\right)^{\alpha_N}
+
\left(\frac{D_c}{D_{\max}}\right)^{\alpha_D},
$$

where $L_{\infty}$ is the irreducible loss, and $N_c$, $D_c$, $\alpha_N$, and $\alpha_D$ are fitted constants.<ref>{{#cite:Q3174}}</ref> The [[data wall]] is the regime in which further gains must come primarily from $N$, [[algorithmic efficiency]], or [[synthetic data]], rather than from additional human-written text.<ref>{{#cite:Q3181}}</ref>

== Inference ==

At inference time, an LLM generates text by repeatedly sampling or selecting a token according to the conditional distribution $P(x_t \mid x_{1:t-1}; \theta)$ and appending it to the context. Decoding strategies such as greedy search, beam search, temperature sampling, and top-$p$ (nucleus) sampling trade off diversity against coherence.<ref>{{#cite:Q3198}}</ref> The computational cost of self-attention grows quadratically with context length, motivating techniques such as [[KV caching]] and efficient attention variants.<ref>{{#cite:Q3130}}</ref>

For a context of length $T$, causal [[self-attention]] computes a $T\times T$ score matrix, so its time and memory costs scale as

$$
\mathcal{O}(T^2d)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathcal{O}(T^2),
$$

respectively, where $d$ is the hidden dimension. [[KV caching]] removes redundant recomputation of past keys and values during autoregressive decoding, reducing the per-token attention cost from $\mathcal{O}(T^2d)$ to $\mathcal{O}(Td)$, at the expense of storing $2Td$ cached scalars per layer.<ref>{{#cite:Q3192}}</ref>

At each decoding step, a token is sampled from

$$
x_t \sim P(x_t\mid x_{1:t-1}; \theta).
$$

Temperature sampling replaces $P$ by

$$
P_\tau(x_t\mid x_{1:t-1})
=
\frac{\exp(z_{x_t}/\tau)}
{\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(z_v/\tau)},
$$

where $z_v$ is the logit assigned to vocabulary entry $v\in\mathcal{V}$, and $\tau>0$ is the temperature. Top-$p$ (nucleus) sampling restricts the support to the smallest set $\mathcal{S}_p$ such that

$$
\sum_{x\in\mathcal{S}_p}
P(x\mid x_{1:t-1})
\ge p.
$$
